newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia gold sector revamp has output in mind.
newsitem.headline: Russia gold sector revamp has output in mind.

text.p: Russia took steps to create its own gold market on Wednesday by freeing bullion prices and preparing to allow some banks to export gold, moves which industry sources said were designed to help the state find cash for mines.

But the changes are unlikely to mean more Russian gold on world markets or an immediate rise in output since some export controls remain and the central bank seems keen to build reserves rather than encourage exports.

"We have freed state price controls on the precious metals market," Sergei Kyshtymov, head of the Central Bank of Russia's precious metals directorate, told a briefing, announcing the bank had begun daily quotes of gold, silver and platinum prices for domestic commercial banks licenced to trade.
Kyshtymov said the bank would next week authorise certain commercial banks to export gold. Some banks have long sought this ability in order to raise cash abroad for mining and other ventures.
The bank has said it plans to acquire most domestic output this year as it did last year, ensuring control over supplies.
Russia was the world's fifth largest gold producer in 1995 when it produced 142 tonnes. But in recent years output has fallen and risk-averse foreign miners have stayed clear.
Various government and union officials see Russia's 1997 gold output in the range of 80-110 tonnes, down from the 122-124 tonnes reported in 1996.
The cash-strapped state no longer has enough cash to finance output. Foreign miners have stayed away and domestic mines are often uninterested in output financed by commercial banks.
"I don't know what they have in mind but I wouldn't be at all surprised if it has to do with attracting foreign investment from overseas," said Rhona O'Connell of T. Hoare & Co in London.

Russia's central bank, bucking a trend, is set on acquiring rather than selling gold. Central bank reserves were about 397 tonnes as of March-April and valued at $2.5 billion. The government keeps another 24.8 tonnes in separate reserves.
The bank said in March it it aimed to boost reserves by 90 tonnes a year, or nearly 25 percent, over 1997 and 1998.

The stockpiling may be linked to President Boris Yeltsin's promise to the International Monetary Fund in the early years of reform to keep reserves at a certain level as a sign of the Kremlin's commitment to market economy changes.

Kyshtymov said central bank gold bids would be the London evening fix minus two percent and offers would be the fix plus two percent -- which could help the bank raise cash at a time when Moscow is keen to get additional revenue.

The central bank, vying with the Finance Ministry and other goverment bodies for control over the lucrative precious metals sector, has said it wants a liquid domestic market and that new price and export rules would not send gold abroad.
Russian commercial banks now hold a mere five tonnes of gold, or about four percent of Russia's 1996 output.
The new trading rules cover deals between certain commercial banks and the central bank. Private citizens were recently allowed to buy and sell very small amounts of gold domestically.

In April, Japanese metals traders in Tokyo said visiting Russian central bank officials were keen to widen the bank's influence and were discussing using gold to back Russian government bond issues. The central bank declined then to comment.
The bonds would probably have mobilised but not sold off gold, which would fit with what analysts have said is Moscow's strategy of boosting, not depleting, gold reserves.
